title: Predicting High Income from Census Attributes
text:
Predicting High Income from Census Attributes
A developer log on tabular ML, fairness, and interpretability
This book is a narrative rewrite of my end-to-end machine learning study on the UCI Adult (Census Income) dataset. I built a reproducible pipeline, compared classical and neural models, evaluated a final LightGBM classifier on a held-out test set, and then asked the harder questions: what features drive predictions, and do error rates differ across demographic subgroups?
The original academic report and PDF (release copy) are unchanged. This site reuses the same exported figures and tables - no pipeline rerun required to read it.

title: Predicting High Income from Census Attributes
text:
0.3 Reproducing the underlying work
Source code, configs, and pipeline scripts live in the GitHub repository. If you want to regenerate artifacts from scratch, start with the README quick-start - this book only points at the exported results.
Rule I followed throughout: never tune or select models on the held-out test set. Selection uses 5-fold CV macro F1 on the training split only.
Let’s start with why I picked this dataset and what the raw census rows looked like after cleaning.

title: 2  The Setup & The Data
text:
2.1 Why this dataset, why this question
Income classification from census variables is a classic benchmark, but I was less interested in beating a leaderboard and more interested in walking through the full lifecycle: cleaning, EDA, model comparison, held-out evaluation, interpretability, and fairness checks. The label is simple - does annual income exceed $50,000? - but the path from raw CSV to a defensible conclusion is not.
My main question, in plain language: how well can I predict high income from demographic, education, employment, and financial attributes, and what do preprocessing choices, model family, calibration, and subgroup diagnostics tell me about how much to trust the result?
I set four concrete goals along the way:

title: 2  The Setup & The Data
text:
Build a leakage-aware, reproducible binary classification dataset.
Compare classical models and neural MLP variants under the same split and metric protocol.
Check whether stronger predictive performance trades off against interpretability or subgroup disparity.
Produce an evidence-first write-up where every claim points to a figure or table.

title: 2  The Setup & The Data
section: 2.2 How I would pick a winner
text:
2.2 How I would pick a winner
Before touching any models, I decided on the selection rule: mean 5-fold cross-validated macro F1 on the training split only. The held-out test set would be used once, at the end, for the selected model. Hyperparameters would come from randomized search on training data. The test set would never influence selection or tuning - that was non-negotiable.

title: 2  The Setup & The Data
text:
2.3 Fetching and defining the task
I fetched the data reproducibly from the UCI ML Repository (id=2) via ucimlrepo. The prediction task is binary: income <= $50K (label 0) vs income > $50K (label 1).
Cleaning was where I hit my first real friction. The raw files use ? as a missing-value token, not proper NA values. I replaced those, dropped duplicates, and encoded the target as 0/1. After cleaning, the analysis dataset contained 48,813 rows and 15 columns.

text:
2.4 First look at missingness
Once the basics were in place, I audited missingness column by column. Several categorical fields still had gaps after replacing ?, which told me imputation strategy would matter downstream.






Figure 2.1: Missing values by column (Figure 1)



Several categorical fields show missing values after the ? -> NA conversion. I made a mental note: mode imputation inside cross-validation folds, never fit on test data.

title: 2  The Setup & The Data
section: 2.5 A quick caveat before going further
text:
2.5 A quick caveat before going further
The Adult dataset reflects a specific U.S. census-era survey population. Labels are coarse (two income bands), and features may encode historical social structure. Everything I report describes associative patterns in this dataset only - I am not claiming the model generalizes to other populations or time periods. A longer discussion of what would be needed for 2026-era use is in Chapter 4 and the external validity essay.
With the data loaded and cleaned, the next step was to actually look at what the census rows contained before training anything.

title: 3  Exploring the Census
text:
3.1 What I kept in the feature set
I retained fourteen input features: six numeric (age, fnlwgt, education-num, capital-gain, capital-loss, hours-per-week) and eight categorical (workclass, education, marital-status, occupation, relationship, race, sex, native-country). A sample of the feature dictionary is below; the full table lives in reports/tables/table_02_feature_dictionary.csv.
I flagged sex and race as sensitive attributes for fairness auditing later. They stayed in the primary modeling pipeline; I tested removal separately in Chapter 4.

title: 3  Exploring the Census
text:
3.2 Numeric separation between income classes
I stratified numeric distributions by the income label to see which continuous fields actually moved. Age, education-num, and hours-per-week showed visible separation between classes. Capital-gain was sparse but jumped out as informative for high earners when it was non-zero.






Figure 3.1: Numeric feature distributions stratified by income label (Figure 4)



That pattern matched my intuition: income in this dataset correlates with experience, education level, and work intensity. I did not drop any numeric field at this stage.

title: 3  Exploring the Census
text:
3.3 Education and correlation structure
Next I wanted to see the impact of education, so I plotted the high-income rate by education level. The result was interesting because Doctorate and Prof-school levels heavily dominated, as shown in Figure 3.2. Tree models would almost certainly lean on education-related splits.






Figure 3.2: Income rate by education level (Figure 5)



I also checked numeric correlation. Features showed moderate correlation, but I did not drop anything solely for collinearity - tree-based models handle redundancy, and I wanted the same feature set across model families for a fair comparison.






Figure 3.3: Numeric correlation heatmap (Figure 6)

title: 3  Exploring the Census
section: 3.4 Feature selection - or the lack of it
text:
3.4 Feature selection - or the lack of it
I deliberately skipped a separate univariate filter beyond EDA. All fourteen inputs feed a unified ColumnTransformer: median/mode imputation, standardisation for numeric fields, one-hot encoding for categoricals. Keeping one consistent pipeline made cross-validation leakage-safe and model comparison cleaner.

title: 3  Exploring the Census
section: 3.5 Class imbalance - the number that changed my metrics
text:
3.5 Class imbalance - the number that changed my metrics
Only 23.9% of records are positive (income > $50K). At this point I realised accuracy alone would be misleading: a naive majority-class classifier could look good while failing high earners. I committed to reporting macro F1 and balanced accuracy alongside accuracy for the rest of the project.






Figure 3.4: Target class distribution (Figure 2)

title: 3  Exploring the Census
text:
3.6 Sensitive attributes and base-rate differences
I then looked at high-income rates by sex and race. The gaps were obvious - different groups enter the dataset with different base rates of earning above $50K. That does not tell me a model will be unfair, but it warned me to run subgroup diagnostics after training.






Figure 3.5: Income rate by sex (Figure 3a)









Figure 3.6: Income rate by race (Figure 3b)



Imbalance plus group rate differences foreshadowed everything in the back half of this project: macro-averaged metrics during tuning, and explicit fairness tables on the test set after selection.
EDA answered what was in the data. The next step was building a leakage-safe pipeline to learn from it.

title: 4  The Modeling Journey
text:
4.1.1 Train/test split
I used a stratified 80/20 split: 39,050 training and 9,763 test records. Positive rates aligned at 23.9% in both splits, which was exactly what I wanted.



Table 4.1: Stratified train/test split summary

4.1.2 Preprocessing inside the pipeline
Preprocessing lives in src/adult_income_ml/pipelines.py:

Numeric: median imputation + standardisation
Categorical: mode imputation + one-hot encoding (handle_unknown="ignore")

The preprocessor is fitted only on training folds inside each CV split (or on the full training set for the final fit). The test set never touches imputation statistics, scaling, or hyperparameter selection. That discipline sounds tedious until you have seen leakage inflate scores once.


4.1.3 Tuning protocol

Search: RandomizedSearchCV (up to 20 iterations per model)
CV: 5 folds on training data
Primary scoring: macro F1
Candidates: dummy baseline, logistic regression, decision tree, random forest, HistGradientBoosting, XGBoost, LightGBM, sklearn MLP, PyTorch embedding MLP

Per-model learning curves were not exported for every family; CV scores and best hyperparameters carry the comparison.

title: 4  The Modeling Journey
section: 4.2 Did more data help? Learning curves
text:
4.2 Did more data help? Learning curves
Before comparing final CV scores, I wanted to see whether models were still gaining from more training rows or starting to plateau. I plotted learning curves on the training split only (macro F1 vs training set size, 5-fold CV).






Figure 4.1: Logistic regression learning curve (Figure 7)



Logistic regression improved steadily with more data but plateaued below the boosting models. That told me a linear decision boundary was not the main bottleneck - data volume was not the issue, capacity was.






Figure 4.2: Random forest learning curve (Figure 8a)









Figure 4.3: LightGBM learning curve (Figure 8b)



Random forest and LightGBM both benefited from additional rows, with LightGBM holding a consistent edge at every training size. That reinforced my plan to focus on boosting for the final selection.

title: 5  Under the Hood & Final Thoughts
text:
5.1 Final evaluation - one pass on the test set
I evaluated the selected LightGBM pipeline once on the held-out test set. Test macro F1 (0.818) landed close to CV macro F1 (0.815), which suggested reasonable generalisation without severe overfitting on this split.
ROC-AUC (0.930) indicated strong ranking ability; PR-AUC (0.836) reflected solid performance on the minority positive class relative to a random baseline.

section: 5.2 Interpretability - what the model actually used
text:
5.2 Interpretability - what the model actually used

5.2.1 Permutation importance
I shuffled each raw input column and measured the drop in macro F1. The largest decreases landed on marital-status, capital-gain, education-num, and age - exactly the kind of signals I expected after EDA.






Figure 5.4: Permutation importance on test data (Figure 13)





5.2.2 SHAP values
The SHAP summary plot now uses human-readable feature labels (for example education: Bachelors, marital-status: Married-civ-spouse) instead of opaque encoded indices. The global pattern was clear: education, marital status, occupation, and age-related splits dominated the tree model’s decisions.






Figure 5.5: SHAP summary for LightGBM (Figure 14)



What struck me was how concentrated the importance was - a handful of columns carried most of the signal, consistent with the education and occupation patterns I saw in EDA.


5.2.3 Representative errors
Looking at concrete mistakes helped more than aggregate scores:

False positives (predicted > $50K, actual <= $50K) often involved married individuals in managerial or professional occupations with moderate hours - profiles that resemble high earners but fall below the threshold in the label.
False negatives (predicted <= $50K, actual > $50K) included professionals with education and occupation signals the model underweighted relative to other constraints.

Errors clustered at the decision boundary of a coarse income band. The model leans on occupation, education, and family-status proxies.

title: 5  Under the Hood & Final Thoughts
section: 5.4 Fairness constraints I did not tune (and why)
text:
5.4 Fairness constraints I did not tune (and why)
Strong test macro F1 did not mean the model treated groups equally. I measured recall gaps, but I did not apply fairness constraints during training. That was deliberate: constraint methods (demographic parity, equalized odds, equal opportunity) need a validation set for threshold or model selection, and this project held out a single test set for one final evaluation.
Demographic parity would ask for similar positive prediction rates across groups, but the dataset itself has very different base rates of high income by sex and race. Equalized odds would push false positive and false negative rates to align across groups - a reasonable production goal, but one that can trade off against overall accuracy. I documented these definitions and the tradeoffs in the fairness constraints essay.
In a deployment setting, I would add a validation fold, define tolerances with stakeholders, and monitor subgroup metrics over time rather than reporting a single aggregate F1 once.

title: 5  Under the Hood & Final Thoughts
section: 5.5 What would it take to use this in 2026?
text:
5.5 What would it take to use this in 2026?
The Adult dataset is not a snapshot of today’s labour market. It reflects 1994 census extraction patterns, a fixed $50K income band without inflation adjustment, and feature definitions from a different economic era. Remote work, gig employment, credential inflation, and shifting immigration patterns all mean the joint distribution of features and labels would differ materially if we collected similar data today.
Using this model for hiring, credit, or benefits screening in 2026 would require new representative data, inflation-adjusted or multi-band labels, modern feature schemas, subgroup monitoring in production, and legal review - not a redeploy of a 1994-era classifier with 0.818 macro F1. I wrote a longer essay on external validity and a revalidation protocol for anyone evaluating whether this benchmark generalizes beyond its historical context.

5.6 Calibration - can I trust the probabilities?
The Brier score is 0.087 (lower is better). The reliability curve compares mean predicted probability to observed positive rate across bins.






Figure 5.8: Calibration curve (Figure 17)



The model is reasonably well calibrated in mid-to-high probability ranges; extreme bins deserve caution due to smaller bin counts. For ranking and threshold analysis, the probabilities seem usable - policy deployment would need more validation.

title: 5  Under the Hood & Final Thoughts
text:
5.8 What I learned
Several methodological lessons stuck with me:

Leakage control - Fitting preprocessing inside CV and holding out one test set avoided optimistic bias. Labelling “CV (train only)” vs “test” explicitly matters in every write-up.
Metric choice - With ~24% positives, accuracy alone would mask poor minority-class performance; macro F1 and PR-AUC were more informative.
Model family - Gradient boosting (especially LightGBM) outperformed linear, single-tree, and embedding MLP models on this tabular data.
Fairness vs accuracy - Strong overall metrics coexist with subgroup recall gaps; fairness auditing is a separate step from tuning one number.
Traceability - Linking claims to artifacts made the project auditable and easier to revise into this developer log.
crumbs: 5  Under the Hood & Final Thoughts

title: 5  Under the Hood & Final Thoughts
text:
5.9 Conclusion
Income above $50K can be predicted with substantial accuracy from census attributes in the Adult dataset: the selected LightGBM model achieves test macro F1 of 0.818 and ROC-AUC of 0.930, using a leakage-safe pipeline and CV-based model selection.
Model family matters - boosting ensembles clearly outperform logistic regression and a PyTorch embedding MLP. Interpretability tools confirm reliance on education, occupation, and demographic proxies. Fairness diagnostics reveal unequal recall and error rates across sex and race subgroups. Calibration is reasonable (Brier 0.087), and removing sex/race reduces performance while proxy features remain informative.
I would answer the main research question in the affirmative for predictive strength within this dataset - with important caveats on subgroup reliability, historical data limits, and non-causal fairness metrics. Future work could include threshold tuning for equalised odds, richer fairness constraints, calibration refitting, and external validation on contemporary survey data.






Limitations I am carrying forward




Historical data: UCI Adult reflects a specific U.S. survey era; patterns may not transfer today.
Coarse labels: Binary income bands hide within-class heterogeneity.
Fairness metrics: Subgroup FPR/FNR/recall describe this model on this test split - not causal fairness guarantees.
Interpretability: SHAP and permutation importance operate on encoded features.
Neural models: The PyTorch embedding MLP was not fully optimised; underperformance is not a definitive ceiling for neural tabular methods.



The original academic report and PDF remain unchanged alongside this narrative rewrite.
